MC: Think Python, Chapter 5: Conditionals and Recursion, question 5

Here is the function from one of the exercises in this chapter.

def recurse(n, s):
    if n == 0:
        print(s)
    else:
        recurse(n-1, n+s)

What happens if you call it like this: recurse(-1, 0)?

column3: It does nothing, because n is not positive.
column5: The condition is n == 0, not n <= 0, so a negative n doesn't stop the recursion; it goes to the else branch and makes a recursive call.
It only prints when n is 0, and n goes -1, -2, -3, and so on, so it never gets there.
It would print 0 only if it reached the base case, but starting from -1, subtracting 1 never makes n equal to 0.

column3: It prints nothing and causes a RecursionError.
column5: Because n never equals 0, the base case never runs; the recursion goes on until Python reaches its limit on the number of frames and raises a RecursionError.
